beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about how facial recognition actually works — not a yes-or-no match, but a probability — and when it actually deserves scrutiny.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro / executive-summary card: fellow's name, role, and a one-line summary of the video's thesis

shot.note: Added 2026-08-25 per program feedback: a spoken executive-summary/personal-intro beat carrying the fellow's own on-screen credit (name + role chip) and a one-line thesis summary, distinct from the silent B00 title card that precedes it.

beats.narration_text: Facial recognition is everywhere right now — unlocking your phone, scanning you at the airport, watching you in stores, running in policing systems. And right now, there's real, unresolved disagreement about whether it's being used responsibly.
beats.new_visual_element: Phone, airport, store, and policing icons — facial recognition is everywhere

shot.note: Four context icons (phone/airport/store/badge) appear in sequence, then a question mark / debate framing.

beats.narration_text: Here's the lens I'll use on it, and on any AI system like it: what's it used for, what happens if it's wrong, and how confident is the claim, really? Scrutiny should scale with those answers.
beats.new_visual_element: The reusable lens: three questions, shown before any example — added per PROOF review (framework-first, not narrated after)

shot.note: Three numbered questions appear in sequence, then a low->high stakes gradient bar previewing 'scrutiny scales with the answers.'

beats.narration_text: How confident is the accuracy claim, really? Here's what the system actually does. A camera detects a face, extracts its features into a numerical code called an embedding, and compares that code against a database. The output isn't yes or no — it's a similarity score. A '98 percent match' is a probability, not a certainty.
beats.new_visual_element: Pipeline: detect face, extract embedding, compare to database, output a similarity score — tagged Q3

shot.note: Same pipeline diagram as before, now tagged 'Q3: how confident?' to connect back to the framework beat.

beats.narration_text: Starting with the low-stakes side: assistive tools for visually impaired users, unlocking your own phone, reuniting missing people with their families, and supporting medical diagnosis — if this is wrong, the cost is usually small.
beats.new_visual_element: Legitimate uses, explicitly tagged LOW-STAKES per the framework

shot.note: List-reveal, sage checkmarks, now carrying a visible 'LOW-STAKES' badge tying it to the framework beat.

beats.narration_text: Now the high-stakes side: mass surveillance without consent, and tracking shoppers who never agreed to it — and if this is wrong, there's no undo. Biometric data can't be reset like a password.
beats.new_visual_element: Harmful uses, explicitly tagged HIGH-STAKES per the framework

shot.note: List-reveal, crimson marks, now carrying a visible 'HIGH-STAKES' badge tying it to the framework beat.

beats.narration_text: So, back to accuracy. NIST, the U.S. government's own standards lab, tested 189 algorithms on more than 18 million images. Most showed real accuracy differences across demographic groups — generally worse on women and people with darker skin. But the best-performing algorithms in that same test showed those gaps shrink to nearly nothing. The Security Industry Association argues the disparity is overstated — NIST's own data says it's real for most systems, just not the top tier.
beats.new_visual_element: NIST FRVT bar chart; dissent now explicitly attributed to the Security Industry Association on screen, per PROOF review

shot.note: [VERIFY: NISTIR 8280, see FACTCHECK.md] Bar chart: most-algorithms gap vs. best-performing near-zero gap; dissent line now names the Security Industry Association directly, not 'some industry voices.'

beats.narration_text: Notice the shape of that: a number that looks precise can feel like a settled fact — the same trap as a fluent AI paragraph. A match score isn't one. It needs human judgment before anyone trusts it.
beats.new_visual_element: The fluency trap: a precise-looking number can feel like a settled fact when it's a probability

shot.note: Side-by-side: a fluent AI sentence and a '98% match' score, both 'looks certain' -> both 'a probability, not a fact.'

beats.narration_text: Try the lens on one real case: a retail store wants facial recognition for loss prevention. What's it for? Catching theft, by scanning every shopper without consent. What happens if it's wrong? An innocent person gets flagged, maybe banned, never told why. How confident is the claim? The vendor says '99% accurate' — the same kind of number that needs the same skepticism as before. Three high-stakes answers. That system needs real scrutiny.
beats.new_visual_element: Worked example (added per PROOF review): the three framework questions applied live to a retail loss-prevention case

shot.note: Three Q&A rows reveal in sequence (used for / what if wrong / how confident), each answer tagged high-stakes, ending on 'needs real scrutiny.'

beats.narration_text: Your turn: pick one AI system you used this week, and ask it those three questions — what it's for, what happens if it's wrong, and how confident the claim really is. If the answers are low-stakes, let it go. If even one is high-stakes, that's where your scrutiny belongs.
